claims.text: Premelting and melting in equimolar CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles are governed by the degree of atomic chemical homogeneity.
Highly homogeneous nanoparticles possess uniformly strong bonds.
High atomic homogeneity delays premelting.
High atomic homogeneity produces a sharper melting transition.
Chemical inhomogeneity produces localized clusters or defects that lower local activation barriers and initiate premelting at lower temperatures.
Equimolar CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles can be synthesized by liquid-phase ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation.
The laser-ablated CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles used as the initial material have sizes between 5 nm and 30 nm.
Rapid quenching ensures high atomic homogeneity in CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles.
Controlled post-synthesis annealing can deliberately induce atomic chemical inhomogeneity in CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles.
STEM-EDS mapping can precisely quantify the degree of atomic homogeneity relevant to the proposed melting mechanism.
Atomic inhomogeneity creates localized defects and variability in bond energies.
Localized defects and bond-energy variability lower the activation barrier for atomic rearrangements contributing to premelting.
A homogeneous atomic distribution maintains a more uniform energy barrier for melting.
More homogeneous, rapidly quenched nanoparticles will have a higher premelting onset temperature than annealed, inhomogeneous nanoparticles.
More homogeneous, rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit a more abrupt DSC melting transition than annealed, inhomogeneous nanoparticles.
The predicted homogeneity-dependent trend holds for equimolar CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles throughout the 5–30 nm size range.
Liquid-phase ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation provides a relatively chemically homogeneous rapid-quench baseline.
Applicability beyond equimolar CoCrFeMnNi or under substantially different processing conditions is uncertain.
Annealing may alter defects or other microstructural features in addition to chemical homogeneity, creating potential confounding factors.

The hypothesis is falsified if samples with confirmed, significantly different chemical homogeneity show no statistically significant difference in premelting or melting onset or transition shape relative to the baseline.
